opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The name actually carries quite a bit of meaning for us.

When we started the project, we were thinking about what a world model really is. It's a model that tries to understand and simulate the physical world: how objects move, how light bounces, how things collide, fall, and interact. We wanted a name that captured that ambition. "Cosmos" refers to the universe as an ordered system, a world that follows rules. That's exactly what we hope the model learns: not just pretty pixels, but the underlying structure and regularity of how the physical world behaves.

There's also a sense of scale in the word. The physical world is enormous and diverse. A robot in a warehouse, a car on a highway, a person cooking in a kitchen all live in the same universe governed by the same physics. We wanted one foundation that could serve all of these physical AI applications, rather than a narrow model for each one. "Cosmos" felt like the right word for something that broad.

And honestly, part of it is aspiration. We are very far from a model that truly understands the whole universe. Today's world models still make lots of mistakes. Objects disappear, physics gets violated. But naming it Cosmos reminds us where we're trying to go. It sets the north star.

Finally, it's about the platform being open. We released Cosmos so developers and researchers could build on it, fine-tune it, and post-train it for their own robots or vehicles. We like the image of a cosmos as something many people can explore, not something one company owns. So the name reflects both the technical goal of simulating the physical world and the community vision around it.

r001.rationale: It says Cosmos aims to understand and simulate the physical world and support broad physical AI applications.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention Sora or contrast Cosmos with creator-oriented early demos.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. Honestly, when we were picking the name, we wanted something that captured what we were really trying to build. A world model, at its core, is trying to learn how the physical world works. How things move, how light falls on surfaces, how objects collide and deform, how time flows forward. That is a very big ambition, and the word "cosmos" carries that sense of everything. It is the whole physical universe and the laws that govern it.

There is also a second layer to it. Our goal with Cosmos is not just to make a single model. It is to build a platform that the whole ecosystem can use, so that people working on robotics, autonomous vehicles, and other forms of physical AI do not each have to start from scratch. A cosmos is a system where many things coexist and interact. We liked that it suggests an open foundation that many different worlds and applications can grow out of.

And I will admit, there is a bit of an engineering aspiration in it too. Physical AI has been held back for a long time because we simply do not have enough data from the real world. Collecting it is slow, expensive, and sometimes dangerous. If a model can learn the underlying structure of reality well enough, you can generate the experiences a robot needs to learn from. So the name is a reminder of the scale of the problem we are trying to solve. We are not trying to simulate one scene or one task. We want to simulate the world, and the name should reflect how seriously we take that.

r001.rationale: The response says Cosmos aims to learn how the physical world works and simulate the world to support physical AI, connecting the name to NVIDIA’s physical-world ambition.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention Sora or contrast Cosmos with creator-oriented positioning in Sora’s early demos.

astra-6.text: To me, Cosmos suggests the ambition to model the physical world as a connected whole. A world model needs to capture more than what a scene looks like—it needs to understand how that scene can evolve, how objects interact, and what happens when an action is taken. The name fits that broad scope. It points toward models that can help AI reason about the world and learn to act within it.

sol-6.1.text: I think Cosmos is a fitting name because it suggests a world governed by physical laws. That captures the ambition of a world model: to learn how things move, interact, and change over time, rather than simply generate individual images. For physical AI, that understanding matters. A robot or an autonomous vehicle needs to anticipate what might happen next and how its actions could affect the world. The name reflects that broader goal.
